briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Growth Mode: Michigan Chains Expand Out-of-State as DEA Rescheduling and Psychedelics Hit Full Speed
briefs.top: Michigan operators are pushing past the 24% wholesale tax with out-of-state growth and hospitality bets, while nationally the DEA rescheduling case has reached closing arguments and the FDA is fast-tracking psilocybin and MDMA-class therapies toward approval. Add a hostile-takeover fight between Curaleaf and Aurora Cannabis, and the industry's consolidation and credibility wave keeps building.

local.text: The company announced a deal last week to acquire Sonoran Roots and its eight Ponderosa brand dispensaries, which will soon make JARS the largest dispensary chain in Arizona. A Michigan-born chain punching into a new state is a signal worth watching for any Michigan brand eyeing multistate growth.

Fields Cannary's Muskegon buildout shows that ambitious hospitality-driven cannabis retail is still moving forward in the state, proof that dispensary-restaurant concepts can still pencil out even under tax pressure.

Jars Cannabis, a retail chain with reportedly 54 stores across Michigan, Arizona, and Colorado, reached an agreement with Madison Heights city authorities to remove a Flock surveillance camera that had been aimed at the store's parking lot entrance. A messy municipal dispute gets resolved in the operator's favor.

Choice Labs is relaunching in August under the name "Intrinsic." The rebrand will reportedly involve scrubbing the old names from its products entirely, with one exception: Choice Chews will keep its name because it's still the best-selling gummy in the state. Smart brand refresh that protects the hero SKU while modernizing the rest of the shelf.

Michigan's wholesale tax is driving closures and a repeal bill, and the gap between operators who can negotiate supply-side relief and those who cannot is becoming a dividing line for survival — but the fact a repeal bill is actively moving, alongside continuing MiCIA litigation, keeps a legislative and legal path to relief alive for operators who can hold on.

national.text: The federal rescheduling case reached its closing-argument stage in late August, pushing the DEA's Schedule III decision closer than ever after years of delay — a milestone that could reshape banking, taxes, and interstate commerce for the whole industry.

The FDA issued national priority vouchers to three companies studying psychedelic-based medicines: psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression, psilocybin for major depressive disorder, and methylone, a drug similar to MDMA, for PTSD. Vouchers like this compress FDA review timelines dramatically, a real accelerant for the psychedelics sector.

Compass Pathways confirmed commercial launch-readiness on track for end of 2026, with launch expected in the first half of 2027, after its second Phase 3 trial confirmed a durable psilocybin treatment response for treatment-resistant depression — the clearest signal yet that a legal psychedelic medicine is close to market.

The House of Representatives is expected to take up Senate-passed legislation to delay the scheduled federal recriminalization of hemp THC products, giving lawmakers more time to craft regulations as an alternative to prohibition. A near-term crisis for hemp-derived brands looks like it's getting punted in favor of a real regulatory framework.

Aurora Cannabis is formally urging shareholders to reject Curaleaf Holdings' unsolicited takeover bid, arguing the offer undervalues the company; Aurora's board unanimously recommended shareholders take no action on the September 2 announcement. A hostile fight, but one that underscores how much scale and international medical cannabis assets are now worth to the biggest U.S. operators.
